Editorial tooling in action

A prose-linting gate that runs on every push.

Vale runs locally and in CI across the MkDocs project above — Microsoft's style rules and write-good's plain-language checks, plus four custom rule sets I wrote myself for this docs set.

BannedWords.ymlHedgeWords.ymlThroatClearing.ymlTriadPadding.ymlMicrosoft stylewrite-good
(.venv) PS C:\...\DOCS-AS-CODE-PROJECT-05> vale docs 78:89 error Use 'they're' instead of 'they are'. Microsoft.Contractions 78:94 suggestion 'are dismissed' looks like passive voice. Microsoft.Passive 94:34 warning 'are listed' may be passive voice. write-good.Passive 97:31 error Remove the spaces around ' – '. Microsoft.Dashes ✗ 153 errors, 93 warnings and 247 suggestions in 18 files.

This isn't a one-time cleanup — it's a standing gate. Every push runs the same check in GitHub Actions, so editorial quality doesn't depend on someone catching it by eye.

Structured authoring

DITA XML — one source, reused everywhere.

A sample end-user guide built the way enterprise docs teams actually work: typed topics, a bookmap for structure, and OASIS-standard reuse mechanisms in place of copy-paste.

Challenge

Flat, duplicated documentation is expensive to maintain — the same caution note, product name, and near-identical install steps end up copy-pasted across files and drift out of sync every time something changes.

Approach

Built a small DITA project — a bookmap, typed topics (task, concept, reference, glossary), and standard reuse mechanisms — so shared content lives in one place and gets pulled in wherever it's needed.

Outcome

One set of topics that can publish to a PDF manual, an HTML help center, or a knowledge base with zero duplicated content and consistent terminology — the pattern enterprise teams use to scale documentation.

Information architecture
  • OBS Studio Quick Start bookmap
    • Preface frontmatter
    • Getting Started concept
      • Installing OBS Studio task
      • Creating Your First Scene task
    • Recording chapter
      • Recording a Video task
      • Output Settings Reference reference
      • Common Recording Issues reference
    • Glossary backmatter
      • Scene glossentry
      • Source glossentry
      • Encoder glossentry
Reuse in practice
Content reuse — conref

The install topic's caution note is pulled in from a shared file instead of retyped — update it once, it updates everywhere it's referenced.

Conditional filtering — platform

Windows and macOS install steps live in the same task topic, filtered by a platform attribute, so one topic serves both operating systems.

Key-based referencing — keyref

The product name is inserted via a key definition throughout every topic — rename the product once, and it updates across the whole guide.

Topic typing

Each topic follows DITA's built-in types — task, concept, reference, glossentry — so structure and formatting stay consistent without manual styling.

Authored in oXygen XML Editor · built with the DITA Open Toolkit (DITA-OT)

View the DITA source 
<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<!DOCTYPE bookmap PUBLIC "-//OASIS//DTD DITA BookMap//EN" "bookmap.dtd">
<bookmap id="obs-guide-bookmap">
  <booktitle>
    <mainbooktitle>OBS Studio Quick Start</mainbooktitle>
    <booktitlealt>Recording Your First Video</booktitlealt>
  </booktitle>
  <bookmeta>
    <author>Documentation Sample</author>
    <bookrights>
      <copyrfirst>
        <year>2026</year>
      </copyrfirst>
      <bookowner>
        <person>Sample Author</person>
      </bookowner>
    </bookrights>
  </bookmeta>

  <frontmatter>
    <preface href="topics/preface.dita"/>
    <keydef keys="product-name">
      <topicmeta>
        <keywords>
          <keyword>OBS Studio</keyword>
        </keywords>
      </topicmeta>
    </keydef>
  </frontmatter>

  <chapter href="topics/concept-scenes-sources.dita" navtitle="Getting Started">
    <topicref href="topics/task-install.dita" navtitle="Installing OBS Studio"/>
    <topicref href="topics/task-create-scene.dita"
      navtitle="Creating Your First Scene"/>
  </chapter>

  <chapter navtitle="Recording">
    <topicref href="topics/task-record-video.dita" navtitle="Recording a Video"/>
    <topicref href="topics/reference-output-settings.dita"
      navtitle="Output Settings Reference"/>
    <topicref href="topics/reference-troubleshooting.dita"
      navtitle="Common Recording Issues"/>
  </chapter>

  <backmatter>
    <booklists> 
    <glossarylist>
      <topicref href="topics/glossentry-scene.dita"/>
      <topicref href="topics/glossentry-source.dita"/>
      <topicref href="topics/glossentry-encoder.dita"/>
    </glossarylist>
    </booklists>
  </backmatter>
</bookmap>

<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<!DOCTYPE task PUBLIC "-//OASIS//DTD DITA Task//EN" "task.dtd">
<task id="task-install">
  <title>Installing <ph keyref="product-name"/></title>
  <shortdesc>Download and install <ph keyref="product-name"/> on Windows or
    macOS.</shortdesc>
  <taskbody>
    <context>
      <p>The installation steps differ slightly by operating system.</p>
    </context>
    <steps>
      <step>
        <cmd>Go to <systemoutput>obsproject.com/download</systemoutput> and download
          the installer for your operating system.</cmd>
      </step>
      <step platform="windows">
        <cmd>Run the downloaded <filepath>.exe</filepath> installer and follow the
          setup wizard, accepting the default options.</cmd>
      </step>
      <step platform="mac">
        <cmd>Open the downloaded <filepath>.dmg</filepath> file, then drag the
          <uicontrol>OBS</uicontrol> icon into your <uicontrol>Applications</uicontrol>
          folder.</cmd>
      </step>
      <step>
        <cmd>Launch <ph keyref="product-name"/>.</cmd>
        <info>On first launch, the Auto-Configuration Wizard runs and recommends
          output settings based on your hardware and internet connection. Accepting
          the recommended settings is a good starting point.</info>
      </step>
    </steps>
    <postreq>
      <note conref="../reuse/shared-content.dita#shared-content/permission-caution"/>
    </postreq>
  </taskbody>
</task>

<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<!DOCTYPE reference PUBLIC "-//OASIS//DTD DITA Reference//EN" "reference.dtd">
<reference id="reference-output-settings">
  <title>Output Settings Reference</title>
  <shortdesc>Key options in the <menucascade><uicontrol>Settings</uicontrol>
    <uicontrol>Output</uicontrol></menucascade> panel, in Advanced output
    mode.</shortdesc>
  <refbody>
    <section>
      <title>Recording settings</title>
      <simpletable relcolwidth="1* 1* 3*" keycol="1">
        <sthead>
          <stentry>Setting</stentry>
          <stentry>Typical value</stentry>
          <stentry>Description</stentry>
        </sthead>
        <strow>
          <stentry>Recording Format</stentry>
          <stentry>mkv</stentry>
          <stentry>Container format. <codeph>mkv</codeph> is recommended during
            recording because it recovers cleanly if OBS crashes or the recording
            is interrupted; remux to <codeph>mp4</codeph> afterward if
            needed.</stentry>
        </strow>
        <strow>
          <stentry>Encoder</stentry>
          <stentry>x264 or hardware (NVENC/QuickSync/AMF)</stentry>
          <stentry>Software encoding (x264) gives the best quality per bit but uses
            more CPU. Hardware encoders use a dedicated chip on the GPU and free up
            CPU for the game or application being captured.</stentry>
        </strow>
        <strow>
          <stentry>Rate Control</stentry>
          <stentry>CBR</stentry>
          <stentry>Constant Bitrate keeps file size predictable and is required for
            most streaming platforms; CRF or a quality-based mode is often preferred
            for local recordings.</stentry>
        </strow>
        <strow>
          <stentry>Bitrate</stentry>
          <stentry>8000&#8211;12000 Kbps (1080p)</stentry>
          <stentry>Higher bitrate improves quality but increases file size and, for
            streaming, requires more stable upload bandwidth.</stentry>
        </strow>
        <strow>
          <stentry>Keyframe Interval</stentry>
          <stentry>2 seconds</stentry>
          <stentry>Most streaming platforms require a keyframe every 2 seconds; leave
            this at the default unless a platform specifies otherwise.</stentry>
        </strow>
      </simpletable>
    </section>
  </refbody>
</reference>
Map organizes chapters, frontmatter, and a glossary list; the task topic reuses shared content via conref and filters steps by platform; the reference topic renders a structured settings table with simpletable.
